title: A Wind Tunnel in a Bicycle Shop

passage.title: A Wind Tunnel in a Bicycle Shop
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
In the autumn of 1901, Wilbur and Orville Wright returned to Dayton, Ohio, feeling discouraged. They had just spent weeks flying a full-sized glider on the sandy dunes of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Before building the glider, the brothers had used math tables printed by flight experts. Those tables told how much lift their cloth wings should produce. Out in the ocean breeze, however, the glider rose only a third as high as the printed charts promised. Wilbur began to suspect that the published air tables were flawed.

Testing new full-sized wings out on the windy coast took months of travel and repair. The brothers needed a way to test dozens of wing shapes right inside their bicycle workshop without waiting for good weather. First, they mounted a small wing and a flat plate onto the front wheel of a bicycle and pedaled fast down a Dayton street. Even that clever test told them that the old math charts were wrong. Still, street gusts were too uneven for exact measurements.

So the brothers built a six-foot wooden trough with a glass viewing window on top. At one end, a belt-driven fan pushed a fast stream of air through a metal honeycomb grid that smoothed out turbulent swirls. Inside the six-foot wooden box in their Dayton shop, miniature wing models cut from sheet steel were tested by Wilbur and Orville against a steady blast of fan air. Each model wing was no larger than a playing card.

To measure how each wing behaved, the brothers crafted two delicate balances out of old hacksaw blades and bicycle spokes. One balance measured lift, the upward force that holds an airplane in the sky. The other balance measured drag, the backward pull of air resistance. Peering through the top glass pane, Orville and Wilbur recorded the exact angle of the balances in notebooks.

Over two winter months, they tested more than two hundred miniature wings of different curves, widths, and thicknesses. Their precise notes proved that long, narrow wings with a gentle curve sliced through the air far better than stubby, thick ones. Armed with their own wind-tunnel data, the Wright brothers built their 1902 glider. It soared smoothly over the dunes and paved the way for the first powered airplane a year later.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"Inside the six-foot wooden box in their Dayton shop, miniature wing models cut from sheet steel were tested by Wilbur and Orville against a steady blast of fan air."

In this sentence, who or what actually performed the action of testing the miniature wing models?

options.text: The six-foot wooden box in the Dayton shop
options.childFeedback: 'Inside the six-foot wooden box in their Dayton shop' only tells WHERE the test happened—the wooden box didn't test the wings by itself!

options.text: Famous flight experts visiting from North Carolina
options.childFeedback: No flight experts visited from North Carolina; Paragraph 1 says the brothers had just returned to Dayton from Kitty Hawk because the experts' printed tables were wrong.

options.text: The sheet steel cutting into the fan blades
options.childFeedback: 'Cut from sheet steel' describes what the miniature wing models were made of—the steel wasn't cutting into the fan blades!

options.text: Wilbur and Orville
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, the passive verb 'were tested by' shows that 'Wilbur and Orville' are the ones who tested the miniature sheet-steel wing models inside the wooden wind tunnel.

questions.provingSentenceText: Inside the six-foot wooden box in their Dayton shop, miniature wing models cut from sheet steel were tested by Wilbur and Orville against a steady blast of fan air.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, the passive verb 'were tested by' shows that 'Wilbur and Orville' are the ones who tested the miniature sheet-steel wing models inside the wooden wind tunnel.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive sentence, 'miniature wing models cut from sheet steel' is the receiver of the verb 'were tested.' The true actors appear right after the preposition 'by': 'Wilbur and Orville' (Option B).
questions.retryHint: Look right after 'were tested by' in Paragraph 3 to see who tested the miniature wing models.

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 1:

"Out in the ocean breeze, however, the glider rose only a third as high as the printed charts promised. Wilbur began to suspect that the published air tables were flawed."

What does the word "flawed" mean as it is used in Paragraph 1?

options.text: Completely proven by every glider flight at Kitty Hawk
options.childFeedback: Completely proven is the exact opposite of 'flawed'! The Kitty Hawk flights rose only a third as high as promised, showing the tables had mistakes.

options.text: Written in a secret code that only pilots could read
options.childFeedback: The air tables were published math charts printed by flight experts for builders to use, not a secret code!

options.text: Inaccurate and containing serious mistakes
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 1, 'flawed' means inaccurate and containing serious mistakes. Because the 1901 glider rose only a third as high as the printed charts promised, Wilbur realized the old math tables were wrong.

options.text: Printed on heavy steel sheets instead of paper
options.childFeedback: The miniature test wings in Paragraph 3 were cut from sheet steel, not the printed math tables in Paragraph 1! 'Flawed' means full of errors.

questions.provingSentenceText: Wilbur began to suspect that the published air tables were flawed.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 1, 'flawed' means inaccurate and containing serious mistakes. Because the 1901 glider rose only a third as high as the printed charts promised, Wilbur realized the old math tables were wrong.
questions.parentExplanation: Because the glider produced far less lift than the printed tables predicted—and Paragraph 2 confirms 'the old math charts were wrong'—'flawed' means inaccurate and containing mistakes (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Look at why Wilbur doubted the printed tables in Paragraph 1 (the glider rose only a third as high as promised) and how Paragraph 2 calls them 'wrong.'

questions.prompt: Why did the Wright brothers place a metal honeycomb grid at the front of their wooden wind tunnel?

options.text: To keep the sheet-steel wings from flying out of the box and hitting the glass window
options.childFeedback: The miniature wings were held in place by balances made of hacksaw blades and bicycle spokes (Paragraph 4), while the honeycomb grid at the front smoothed the incoming fan air.

options.text: To smooth out rough, swirling air from the fan so the wind flowed evenly past the models
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 explains that the belt-driven fan pushed air through a metal honeycomb grid to smooth out rough, swirling air ('turbulent swirls') so a steady, even stream of wind hit the model wings.

options.text: To heat the air inside the bicycle shop during the cold Ohio winter months
options.childFeedback: The honeycomb grid smoothed out swirling fan air inside the six-foot trough; it wasn't a heater for the Dayton bicycle shop!

options.text: To block all air from entering the wooden trough while Orville drew in his notebook
options.childFeedback: Blocking all air from entering the trough would defeat the whole purpose of a wind tunnel! The grid let a fast, steady stream of air pass through.

questions.provingSentenceText: At one end, a belt-driven fan pushed a fast stream of air through a metal honeycomb grid that smoothed out turbulent swirls.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 explains that the belt-driven fan pushed air through a metal honeycomb grid to smooth out rough, swirling air ('turbulent swirls') so a steady, even stream of wind hit the model wings.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 states that 'a belt-driven fan pushed a fast stream of air through a metal honeycomb grid that smoothed out turbulent swirls,' ensuring a steady, even airflow for accurate testing (Option B).
questions.retryHint: Check the second sentence of Paragraph 3 to see what the metal honeycomb grid did to the 'turbulent swirls' from the fan.

questions.prompt: How does the author organize the information across the entire passage?

options.text: By presenting the problem of inaccurate flight tables and tracing how the brothers invented and used a wind tunnel to solve it
options.childFeedback: The passage follows a problem-and-solution structure in time order: Paragraph 1 introduces inaccurate lift tables, Paragraphs 2 through 4 show how the brothers built a wind tunnel, and Paragraph 5 shows how their data solved the problem.

options.text: By comparing the price of bicycles in Dayton to the cost of train tickets to North Carolina
options.childFeedback: The author never mentions bicycle prices or train ticket costs; the passage focuses on how the Wright brothers tested wing shapes.

options.text: By listing two hundred wing shapes in alphabetical order from the worst design to the best design
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 says they tested more than two hundred miniature wings of different curves and widths, not that the article lists two hundred wings in alphabetical order!

options.text: By arguing that bicycle wheels are much easier to build than wooden boxes with glass windows
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 shows that testing a wing on a bicycle wheel outdoors was actually too gusty and uneven, which is why they built the indoor wooden wind tunnel instead.

questions.provingSentenceText: The brothers needed a way to test dozens of wing shapes right inside their bicycle workshop without waiting for good weather.
questions.childTip: The passage follows a problem-and-solution structure in time order: Paragraph 1 introduces inaccurate lift tables, Paragraphs 2 through 4 show how the brothers built a wind tunnel, and Paragraph 5 shows how their data solved the problem.
questions.parentExplanation: The passage follows a clear problem-and-solution chronological structure: Paragraph 1 introduces the problem of flawed lift tables; Paragraphs 2–4 show how the brothers designed their wind tunnel and balances; Paragraph 5 shows how their data solved the problem (Option B).
questions.retryHint: Follow the steps from the glider problem in Paragraph 1 to the wind-tunnel invention in Paragraphs 2–4 and the successful 1902 glider in Paragraph 5.

questions.prompt: PART A: What key discovery did the Wright brothers make by testing two hundred model wings in their wind tunnel?

options.text: Thick, stubby wings made of cloth rose three times higher than thin steel wings.
options.childFeedback: This is the exact opposite of what they found! Paragraph 5 says long, narrow wings with a gentle curve worked far better than stubby, thick ones.

options.text: Long, narrow wings with a gentle curve performed much better in the air than thick, stubby wings.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 states that the Wright brothers' wind-tunnel notes proved that long, narrow wings with a gentle curve sliced through the air far better than thick, stubby ones.

options.text: Famous flight experts had already tested every possible wing shape on a bicycle wheel.
options.childFeedback: It was Wilbur and Orville who tested a small wing on a bicycle wheel in Paragraph 2 after realizing the flight experts' published tables were wrong.

options.text: Gliders could fly without any wings at all if a belt-driven fan was bolted to the front.
options.childFeedback: The belt-driven fan stayed inside the Dayton shop wind tunnel (Paragraph 3); gliders fly over sand dunes using wings and ocean breezes, not without wings!

questions.provingSentenceText: Their precise notes proved that long, narrow wings with a gentle curve sliced through the air far better than stubby, thick ones.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 5 states that the Wright brothers' wind-tunnel notes proved that long, narrow wings with a gentle curve sliced through the air far better than thick, stubby ones.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5RI1, Paragraph 5 explicitly states what their wind-tunnel notes proved: 'long, narrow wings with a gentle curve sliced through the air far better than stubby, thick ones' (Option C).
questions.retryHint: Check the second sentence of Paragraph 5 to see what the brothers' precise notes proved about the best wing shape.
